source.title: Decoding Dense Embeddings: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting and Discretizing Dense Retrieval
source.authors: Seongwan Park; Tae-Kyung Kim; Youngjoong Ko

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a latent-intrusion evaluation to compare the semantic interpretability of SimLM’s ordinary embedding dimensions with SAE-derived features. This bears conceptually on polysemanticity, but it does not test the specified vision or transformer-MLP neuron settings.
record.gate_note: Appendix G reports the study’s own latent-intrusion comparison for SimLM’s 768-dimensional hidden representation and SAE features. Other SAE reconstruction, retrieval, and human-interpretability results do not measure individual-neuron polysemanticity. The study does not inspect the specific mixed-input neuron or determine whether its inputs share a feature the network uses.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on SimLM dense retrieval embeddings and reports its own method's reconstruction, interpretability and retrieval performance. The polysemanticity of neurons is assumed as motivation, citing Olah et al. 2020. The one related check (Appendix G) runs a latent-intrusion test on the 768 output embedding dimensions of a BERT-style retrieval encoder. Those are not MLP neurons, not a vision model, and no cause, architecture or measurement dependence is examined. It is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the authors do not establish that neurons are often polysemantic in their setting. They cite Olah et al. 2020 and say they 'believe this holds in our setting'. They offer the 0.46 vs 0.86 intrusion gap as support for using SAEs. Their main conclusion is that SAE latents interpret DPR embeddings and enable efficient concept-level sparse retrieval (CL-SR).
record.recipe_differences: Uses a latent-intrusion test on dense-retrieval representations and compares standard dimensions with SAE features; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.

fits_no_version.finding: For SimLM's 768 output embedding dimensions, LLM-judged latent-intrusion accuracy was 0.46, versus 0.86 for SAE k=32 latents. Chance is 0.1; no uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard-basis output embedding dimensions of a dense retrieval encoder are less coherent in an intrusion test than SAE latents, though well above chance.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The intrusion result is a proxy for semantic interpretability, not a direct test of whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The paper gives no uncertainty estimate for the 0.46 and 0.86 comparison.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or vision neurons are studied.
No MLP neurons in transformer LMs are measured. Only final embedding dimensions of SimLM are examined, with no layer breakdown and no share of polysemantic units.
Superposition is cited (Elhage et al. 2022) as motivation but not tested.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures or regularization on neuron polysemanticity.
No revisiting of specific mixed neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods for neuron polysemanticity. The LLM-judged intrusion score is used without sensitivity analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'tests'/T2 conflicted with its own assessment that every version is not_tested. It is changed to uses_without_test/T4. Zoom In is cited, but this study is not one of the originals.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses dense retrieval encoders, not image classifiers or vision-model neurons.
It does not measure MLP neurons in transformer language models responding to tokens or contexts.
It does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
It does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
It does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization effects on the share of polysemantic neurons, or test performance costs of lowering that share.
The study does not revisit particular mixed-activation neurons with better tools to determine whether their inputs share one feature or job.
It does not compare neuron-polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: SimLM
rows.operation_detail: Latent-intrusion test on the hidden representation, under the same setting as the SAE comparison.
rows.locator: Appendix G, Comparison with Neuron-based Interpretability
rows.note: The paper compares this result with 0.86 for its SAE-based method and describes the difference as substantial. This measures interpretability in a passage-based intrusion task, not responses of individual model neurons to varied inputs.
rows.check: This measures output embedding dimensions of a retrieval encoder, not MLP neurons. The intrusion test also cannot separate polysemantic from abstract or weakly selective dimensions. 'partial' has no version to be partial against. Chance in the 10-choice test is 0.1, so 0.46 is well above chance; the paper reports no baseline or uncertainty.

rows.locator: Appendix G, Comparison with Neuron-based Interpretability
rows.note: The paper presents this as the SAE-based comparison to the standard hidden representation; the result is for SAE features, not individual neurons.
rows.check: This is the study's own SAE method used as a comparator, not a measurement of neuron polysemanticity, so it should not be a claim row. The value 0.86 matches Table 2's 0.859 for SAE k=32 (other k: 0.829, 0.808, 0.764).
